bearings.paper_claim: Pooled random-effects r per trait: O .39 [.30,.48], C .35 [.29,.42], E .40 [.33,.46], A .29 [.21,.36], N .33 [.27,.39], 16 effect sizes each. Heterogeneity I2 93.15-97.46. Each study contributed its best model or highest single-feature effect. Paper-side numbers reproduced exactly from Table 2 (Z, Q, I2, tau2).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.2.1 p.154; Table 2 p.157; Sec. 2.4 p.152-153; Abstract p.150
bearings.system_side: Code matches the description: closed-vocabulary standardized linear model with corpus z-scoring over member posts plus CREC and INTERVIEW speech (big5_traits.py docstring and source setup). The Birkenmaier citation is in the docstring. NOT FOUND: the held-out CV against RKH (E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214, mean .350). data/members/big5_v2.json holds held-out r against behavioral targets: A .059 (cooperation_z), C .281 (diligence_z), E .563 (visibility_z), O .135 (breadth_z); ES has no held-out r (v1 fallback).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Azucar's pooled r is not a benchmark for this system. Its criterion is self-report from lay users; the system's held-out targets are behavioral dispositions, and no RKH held-out figure exists in the repo. Heterogeneity is over 93 percent and best-model selection probably inflates the pooled values. Any citation must carry the label UNSTRATIFIED (16 studies, 4 platforms, 2012-2017; two included studies, Farnadi 2016 Study 1 and Kosinski 2013, used MyPersonality data). The ordering claim as first written is wrong: in Azucar E (.40) is highest and O (.39) second; A (.29) is lowest. In this system O is the weakest trait on the breadth target (.135), which is not an inversion of a best-predicted trait.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers reproduced. Corrected: E, not O, is the best-predicted trait in Azucar. The RKH CV figures and the mean of .350 appear in no repo artifact and were removed. The claim that O was reversed on the party check: big5_traits.py defines the check (EXP O = -1, lines 276 and 284), but no run output is in the repo, so it is unverified.

bearings.paper_claim: Agreeableness is the least recoverable trait from footprints (r .29 [.21,.36]). A gained no accuracy from multiple footprint types. Among the moderators tested, demographics was the only significant gain for A (beta .25, R2 .19).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.2.1 p.154; Sec. 3.2.3 p.154-155; Discussion Sec. 4 p.155
bearings.system_side: Lexical susceptibility formula is susc = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E (receptivity_layer.py line 189). The default behavioral basis uses .40*coop + .30*reactivity N - .20*dil - .10*dom (line 186). The BASIS comment (lines 58-65) documents that RECEPT_TRAITS=lexical reverts the basis; the default is behavioral.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is about predicting self-report among lay users. It does not test susceptibility to pressure or any choking composite, so it cannot support the susceptibility weights. Its only bearing is that lexical A is the weakest footprint trait. The analyst's statement that the paper supports the system's move from lexical A to behavioral cooperation is the analyst's inference, not the paper's finding.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claims and both code formulas verified at the cited lines. The verdict covers the paper and code citations only; the paper does not speak to the susceptibility model.

bearings.paper_claim: Demographics (age, gender) as a moderator raised accuracy for N (beta .25, p<.05, R2 .19) and A (beta .25, R2 .19). O showed a marginal gain (beta .26, R2 .12, p=.09).
bearings.system_side: affective_n is the LLM affective facets residualized on E, then on party, then z-scored (emit_affective_n.py lines 52-56). The gate comment at line 43 reads party .00. The residualization controls for party and E only; age and gender are not controlled in these lines.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's demographic moderator is between-study and univariate: whether a study used demographic features, with no adjustment. It does not show an individual-level mechanism. The paper says its demographic finding is consistent with survey literature on demographic differences in self-reported traits (Goldberg 1998; Soto 2011). The analyst's claim that the gain comes from group membership correlating with self-reported traits, a predictive shortcut, goes beyond the paper. Do not adopt demographic predictors on the strength of this paper.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers match. Gate and residualization verified in code. The mechanism claim was the analyst's inference and has been rewritten as a hypothesis. The gate controls party, not age or gender.

bearings.paper_claim: Social-media activity statistics (posts, friends, network density, likes received, comments, tags) gave a marginal increase in E accuracy (beta .19, R2 .18, p=.06). The paper reports no other significant moderator effects; it does not report a tested null for each trait.
bearings.system_side: visibility_z is broadcast engagement: log counts of attributed interviews and interview programs, for members with at least 3 interviews (behavioral_dispositions.py line 18; visibility block near lines 111-113). Dominance uses floor turn statistics plus committee leadership. The visibility measure is press-interview engagement, not social-media activity.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The constructs differ. The paper's activity variables are social-media posting, friend counts and network density; the system's variable counts press or broadcast interviews. Any link is an analogy, not support, and it bears on E only, not on the lexical E it was meant to contrast with. The analyst's point that interview counts track press-office scheduling and seniority is their inference and was not checked against the repo.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers verified. The relation 'supports' was not warranted because the measures differ; relation changed to context. The 'no other trait improved' wording was rewritten to match what the paper reports.

bearings.paper_claim: Combining several footprint types gave significant gains for O (beta .27, R2 .16), C (beta .25, R2 .20) and N (beta .21, R2 .14). E showed a trend (beta .18, R2 .12, p=.08). A showed no gain. Text or pictures alone added nothing over other types.
bearings.system_side: The v3 hybrid ridge combines lexical features, 8 interaction-channel features and agency/communion persona cues, with nested 5-fold CV and honest held-out r (big5_hybrid.py docstring lines 3-12; heldout_r lines 46-62). The committed artifact data/members/big5_v3_hybrid.json shows no gain over lexical-only: A hybrid .056 vs lexonly .059; C .273 vs .281; E .564 vs .563; O .130 vs .135. The hybrid docstring says interaction features are nickname-degraded until re-ingest, so these numbers are a floor.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper concerns social-media footprint types measured against self-report among lay users. The hybrid adds interaction-channel features that are not footprint types, and its targets are behavioral. The paper gives no basis for expecting a gain from interaction features. In the system's own output the added features gave no held-out gain on any target, so the paper does not support the current hybrid. Any future claim needs a pre-registered look and second-path reproduction (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers verified. The honest held-out method is verified in code. The 'supports' relation was overstated: the artifact's held-out r equals lexical-only within .01 on every target, so the relation was changed to context.

related.why: Meta-analysis of Big Five against LIWC categories (title and research question verified). Relevant to the closed-vocabulary feature family used in big5_traits.py.
Legislator speech scoring (title verified). The item confirms there is no ground-truth personality inventory for legislators, which is the gap Azucar's lay-user evidence does not fill.

Text measures of politicians' agency and communion from speeches, interviews and social posts (title verified). This is the source the system cites for social posts, and it uses a different construct from Azucar's self-report criterion.
Big Five regression from Twitter text (title verified). Same single-platform design that Azucar pools.
Sampling biases in social network site data (title verified). Bears on Azucar's limitation that samples were mostly English-speaking or Sina Weibo users.
Review of threats, challenges and ethics in personality computing (title verified). Overlaps Azucar's ethics discussion.
2025 survey of machine and deep learning for trait detection (title verified). Covers methods after Azucar's May 2017 search cutoff.

summary_issues: Held-out CV figures are not in the repo: the summary's 'held-out CV against RKH mean .350' and the claim that it sits inside Azucar's range by coincidence should be removed. Repo held-out r in data/members/big5_v2.json are against behavioral targets: A .059, C .281, E .563, O .135; ES has none.

The summary says the pooled numbers are optimistic. The paper does not say that. It says each study contributed its best model or strongest feature, which may inflate the pooled r; rewrite as a possibility.

The summary says demographics improve accuracy only because group membership correlates with self-reported traits. The paper does not establish that mechanism; it cites survey literature on demographic differences in self-report. Rewrite as a hypothesis.
The summary says the affective-N gate removes exactly the demographic signal. The residualization in emit_affective_n.py controls for party and E only; age and gender are not controlled.
The summary says Agreeableness supports the system's move from lexical A to behavioral cooperation. The paper tests no system; at most it is consistent with the move. Reword accordingly.

The summary says Melange's Congress data is staff-written and that the system is validated against Senate expert and insider panels. Neither is in the paper, and neither was checked in the code read here. Mark as unverified.
Bearing 1 says O is the best-predicted trait in Azucar. This is false: E (.40) is highest and O (.39) second. Corrected in the bearing.

The paper's Table 1 asterisks do not match its exclusion text: Farnadi 2016 Study 3 is asterisked but its Twitter data is needed for the 7/5/3/1 platform split, and Golbeck 2016 Study 3 is excluded in the text but not asterisked. The platform split reconciles with the text's inclusion list, so the asterisks should not be used.

The paper's own text says 11 MyPersonality studies plus Golbeck 2016 Study 3 were excluded, and that two MyPersonality-based studies (Farnadi 2016 Study 1; Kosinski 2013) were included. The summary's 'ordinary users' description should note the two included MyPersonality studies.

Paul alignment section: the item has no Paul annotations (paul_entries is empty and the ext coverage notes none found), so attributions to Paul's views and to his receptivity-layer notes cannot be verified. Remove or mark unverified.

Ext note: the Bachrach 2012 ad-targeting claim sits on p.157 (Conclusions), not p.156. The Kosinski 2014 conscientiousness finding is fewer pictures, fewer Likes and less group activity, not a general 'post less'.

Bearing 5 and the flags: the summary's suggestion that the hybrid gives directional support for footprint combination conflicts with the artifact's held-out numbers, which show no gain over lexical-only on any target.
